centuries.life: At the end of the Ice Age some hunters in the Levant stop moving. Natufian families live in round huts on stone footings, some dug into the ground, cut wild barley with flint sickles that the stalks polish to a gloss, and pound acorns and almonds in heavy stone mortars. They bury their dead with shell beads; at Ain Mallaha an elderly person lies with a puppy. A thousand cold, dry years follow, and by about 8300 BC Jericho has raised a stone tower 8.5 metres high.
centuries.food: Wild cereals, wild legumes, almonds, acorns and pistachios, gazelle above all, with waterfowl and fish in the Jordan valley; at Shubayqa in Jordan someone baked a flat bread of wild grain 14,400 years ago.
centuries.smell: A camp smelled of fire and roasting gazelle, and perhaps of fermenting grain: a residue in Raqefet Cave on Mount Carmel, about 13,000 years old, may be the oldest beer.
centuries.trouble: There is no state to quarrel over; the question is food, as the Younger Dryas dries the wild cereal stands from about 10,800 BC and, by one contested theory, pushes people to sow what they once only gathered.

centuries.life: Farming villages now stand from Anatolia to the plains of Henan. Çatalhöyük, founded about 7100 BC on the Konya plain, is a honeycomb of mud-brick houses with no streets: people walk across the roofs and climb down ladders through the smoke hole. Inside, smooth plastered walls carry cattle heads and hunting scenes, and the dead lie folded under the floors and the beds. At Jiahu in Henan, 250 to 800 people grow rice and millet inside a moat and play flutes cut from crane bones.
centuries.food: Several wheats, barley, peas, almonds and pistachios, bread and porridge from domed ovens, beef, mutton, fish and birds at Çatalhöyük; at Jiahu, millet, rice and wild soybeans, with a fermented drink of rice, honey and hawthorn.
centuries.smell: Çatalhöyük smelled of hearth and oven smoke with only the roof hole to leave by, of penned cattle and sheep, and of the middens outside, banked with the ash of wood, reeds and dung.
centuries.trouble: The old equality is tested: Çatalhöyük has no palace and no temple, but in its later levels some households keep more querns and more storage than others.

centuries.life: Farmers have walked into Europe at about four kilometres a year. Along the Danube and the Rhine, Linear Pottery villages of five to eight timber longhouses, wattle and daub under thatch, stand twenty metres apart; one at Bylany runs 45 metres, and a house may last thirty years. In Baluchistan, at Mehrgarh, people store barley in baskets lined with bitumen and wear lapis brought from Badakhshan, and someone there has drilled the molars of the living: the oldest dentistry known.
centuries.food: Einkorn and emmer sown together, later barley and lentils, with beef, pork and milk in the Danube villages; six-row barley, wheat, jujubes and dates, with mutton, goat and beef, at Mehrgarh.
centuries.smell: A longhouse village smelled of oak smoke seeping through the thatch, of cattle, the favourite beast, and of the clay pits dug beside each house for daub.
centuries.trouble: Land and killing: around 5000 BC whole Linear Pottery communities end in massacre pits at Talheim and Schöneck-Kilianstädten, children among the dead, and the population of the region falls for fifteen centuries.

centuries.life: On the loess of the Wei valley, Banpo is a village of 100 to 500 people inside a moat five or six metres wide. Its round houses of mud and timber are sunk a metre into the ground under overhanging thatch; potters fire red bowls painted with black fish and human faces in China’s first kilns. Adults are buried on the northern edge, infants in jars beside the houses. On the Black Sea at Varna, a few graves hold most of three thousand gold objects.
centuries.food: Foxtail millet, the staple of northern China, with pork, dog, hazelnuts, chestnuts and pine nuts, and fish if the pots are to be believed.
centuries.smell: A Banpo village smelled of the kilns firing at a thousand degrees, of pigs and dogs, and of millet husk and wet loess.
centuries.trouble: Rank appears: at Varna about 4500 BC three graves with sceptres hold more than half of the cemetery’s gold, and one man is buried with a mace and a gold sheath, the oldest elite burial known.

centuries.life: In southern Mesopotamia a town becomes a city. Uruk spreads over some 250 hectares and holds 25,000 to 50,000 people; the temples of its Eanna precinct run to 80 metres long. Workers depend on the temple and are paid in barley and wool, the grain probably doled out in mould-made bowls that make up four-fifths of all the pottery found. Before 3300 BC scribes begin to keep accounts on clay. North of the Black Sea, Trypillian farmers live in rings of up to 3,000 houses.
centuries.food: Barley above all, as bread and beer, with dates, legumes and mutton in Sumer; on the Trypillian loess, wheat, barley, millet, peas and beans, with meat only about a tenth of the diet.
centuries.smell: Uruk smelled of the flocks kept for their wool, of bread for the ration lines and of beer in storage jars; a Trypillian town smelled of clay and thatch, and every sixty to eighty years of the whole settlement burning.
centuries.trouble: Who works for whom: Uruk’s administrators feed dependent labourers by ration and list them by age and sex, while on the Trypillian megasites equality holds for a few generations and then frays.

centuries.life: The Nile has one king. Narmer’s heirs rule from Memphis in the double crown, their scribes are learning hieroglyphs and their governors count the harvest, while almost everyone else farms from a house of mud brick, sowing when the flood goes down in October and reaping from March. On the lower Yangtze, Liangzhu walls in some three square kilometres, threaded by thirty kilometres of canals with eight water gates and guarded by dams in the hills; its lords go to the grave under heaps of jade.
centuries.food: Emmer bread ground on saddle querns, gritty enough to wear down the teeth, barley beer every day, onions, garlic, lentils and fish by the Nile; rice from the silos of Liangzhu.
centuries.smell: An Egyptian village smelled of river mud and drying brick, of emmer pounded and spread in the sun, and of beer bread crumbled into water to ferment.
centuries.trouble: The first kingdom asks who owns the harvest and the labour: Egypt’s farmers owe the state work on its canals and buildings, and the realm Narmer joined by war in the Delta already reaches into Canaan and Nubia.

centuries.life: Sumer is a land of about thirteen walled cities, each round its temple and ruled by a lugal or an ensi, its barley and date palms fed by canals. Uruk may hold 50,000 to 80,000 people, and in some districts three people in four live in town. At the north-western edge of the farming world, on Orkney, the families of Skara Brae sit round a central hearth in stone houses with box beds and a stone dresser facing the door, banked against the wind with their own midden.
centuries.food: Barley bread and beer, dates, mutton and goat in Sumer; on Orkney, beef, pork and mutton, barley, fish and shellfish, stored in Grooved Ware jars that hold up to thirty litres.
centuries.smell: Skara Brae smelled of hearth smoke trapped under the roofs and of fish bones and shells in the midden packed round its walls; a Sumerian city of canal water and of sheep and goats brought in from the pastures.
centuries.trouble: Water and boundaries: the cities of Sumer, divided by canals and boundary stones, quarrel over irrigated land, as Lagash and Umma will for generations.

centuries.life: On the desert coast of Peru, in the Supe valley, Caral raises six platform mounds and two sunken round plazas; the largest mound stands 18 metres high, built of stones hauled up in reed bags. Its people make no pottery and have left no trace of war. They irrigate cotton for fishing nets and cloth, keep a knotted-string record, and play flutes of pelican bone. On the Pontic steppe, Yamnaya herders move with ox-drawn wagons and bury their chiefs, coated in ochre, under kurgans.
centuries.food: Squash, beans, sweet potato, guava and lúcuma, roasted, with anchovies, sardines, clams and mussels at Caral, where plants made up more than 70 per cent of the diet; probably meat, milk products and mead on the steppe.
centuries.smell: Caral smelled of food roasted over open fires, since there were no cooking pots, and of anchovies, sardines and shellfish carried up from the Pacific shore.
centuries.trouble: Caral has no walls and no weapons, yet someone commands the labour that piles its mounds; on the steppe the kurgans, mostly for men, show where wealth and power are gathering.

centuries.life: Egypt becomes the Old Kingdom, a state of farmers. Most people live in mudbrick houses built to stay cool by day, each holding one family, and owe the king labour on canals and building sites. At Saqqara, Djoser’s step pyramid rises in stacked mastabas, the world’s first large-scale stone building and the first to stand taller than Jericho’s old tower. Children go naked until about twelve; a third die in infancy, and men who survive can expect to reach about thirty-five.
centuries.food: Bread and beer, onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, dates and figs, with fish and fowl for all but the poorest, and wine and meat on feast days.
centuries.smell: A Nile town smelled of bread baking in clay moulds set in the embers, of onions and garlic, and of the river mud the flood leaves behind.
centuries.trouble: The question is the king’s claim on everyone’s time: farmers are taxed on the land they hold and called out in the corvée to cut canals and haul stone.

centuries.life: On the Indus, cities are built to a plan. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro may each house 30,000 to 60,000 people in courtyard houses of baked brick on a grid, with some 700 wells at Mohenjo-daro, about one for every three houses, and covered drains under the main streets. Most townspeople are traders and craftsmen, shell-cutters and bead-makers, living street by street with their trade. No palace and no great temple has been found; the one public monument is a bath.
centuries.food: Beef, buffalo, goat, pork and chicken with a little dairy, wheat, barley and pulses sown for the winter and rice, millets and beans for the summer.
centuries.smell: A Harappan street smelled of wet brick and of bathwater running into the drains, and of shell and agate dust from the craftsmen’s quarters.
centuries.trouble: The Indus cities leave no sign of kings, and almost every house has water and a drain, which suggests wealth spread unusually evenly; the question that will end them is water itself, as the region slowly dries.

centuries.life: At Giza a town grows beside the pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure, with communal sleeping halls, bakeries, breweries, kitchens, a copper workshop and a hospital. Ten thousand or more labourers, mostly from poor families, rotate through in three-month shifts; they are fed well, and buried with bread and beer in mudbrick tombs beside the king’s. In Sumer, at Ur, the royal dead go to the grave in gold and lapis with their lyres, and with between six and eighty attendants killed to follow them.
centuries.food: Bread, beef and fish for the pyramid crews; barley bread and beer, dates, mutton and goat in Sumer.
centuries.smell: The workers’ town at Giza smelled of bread ovens and breweries, of the copper workshop and of the cattle slaughtered to feed the crews.
centuries.trouble: Who serves and who is served: Egypt’s pyramid crews are paid labourers, not slaves, but the death pits at Ur hold attendants killed, some by blows to the head, to go with their masters.

centuries.life: In Syria, Ebla rules some 200,000 people, 40,000 of them in the capital, from a palace whose archive holds thousands of clay tablets. Its villages own the land and give the palace a yearly share; the kingdom counts about 140,000 sheep and goats and 9,000 cattle, and sends textiles and timber downriver to Kish. In Sumer, Urukagina of Lagash decrees that the rich must pay silver for what they buy from the poor and may not force a sale, and that widows and orphans go untaxed.
centuries.food: Barley bread and beer, the measure of everything: Urukagina’s decree sets 80 loaves and 3 jugs of beer for a burial; at Ebla the palace feeds its permanent and seasonal workers from its own stores.
centuries.smell: Ebla smelled of sheep and goats driven in from the pastures and of the wool and cloth that were its chief trade; a Sumerian town of bread ovens and beer.
centuries.trouble: Debt and land: Urukagina’s reforms, the first known, limit what the rich may take from the poor, while Lagash and Umma fight on over irrigated fields and Ebla wars with Mari for the river trade.

centuries.life: Sargon of Akkad, a king with no royal father, makes himself master of Sumer and boasts that 5,400 men eat before him every day. His officials measure grain into the royal stores by a standard gur of about 300 litres; southern governors pay tax and send labourers, and most work in the great households is done by dependants paid in rations, slaves being few. His grandson Naram-Sin makes himself a god. On the lower Yangtze, the city of Liangzhu is abandoned to the floods.
centuries.food: Barley, measured by the royal gur, as bread and beer, with dates and mutton; the great households pay their dependants in rations of grain.
centuries.smell: An Akkadian city smelled of barley in the royal warehouses, of bread and beer made for the ration lines, and of the goods brought back from Dilmun and Magan.
centuries.trouble: Empire itself is the quarrel: the old city-states rise against Akkad again and again, two of Sargon’s sons may have been murdered, and Naram-Sin calls himself King of the Four Quarters.
src: Wikipedia, Archaeological ruins of Liangzhu City

centuries.life: A drought settles on the old world for most of a century. In northern Mesopotamia the plains empty around 2170 BC and perhaps 300,000 people flee south; the Gutians take Akkad, and a wall 180 kilometres long is raised against the Amorites. In Egypt low Nile floods coincide with the end of royal power: governors make their offices hereditary and raise their own armies, and the warlord Ankhtifi describes a land riven by hunger. In China the Longshan towns of Shandong decline.
centuries.food: Less of everything: in Oman and the Gulf the winter winds salted the irrigated fields and cut the harvest to famine, and in Egypt every local lord claimed to have fed his own province while others went hungry.
centuries.smell: The Near East smelled of dust: the dust laid down in the region records its driest years in centuries, from about 2310 to 2020 BC.
centuries.trouble: Who keeps order when the state fails: Egypt splits between Heracleopolis and Thebes, Akkad falls, and the south walls itself off against the herders while refugees pour in.
src: Wikipedia, First Intermediate Period of Egypt

centuries.life: Ur rebuilds Sumer as a ledger. Under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi the scribes write some 120,000 surviving tablets; one office at Girsu manages 6,000 textile workers, mostly women and children, and the depot at Puzrish-Dagan moves 70,000 sheep in a year. Each province feeds the centre one month in twelve. Men and women in the state workshops are paid in barley and wool, sometimes oil, dates or beer. At Ur the ziggurat rises on a base 60 by 45 metres.
centuries.food: Barley above all, paid out as wages with wool, oil, dates and beer, and sheep by the tens of thousands driven through the state depot.
centuries.smell: Ur smelled of sheep pens and wool, of the looms of the state workshops and of barley being measured out by the royal gur.
centuries.trouble: The state’s grip and its limits: the bala tax rotates through the provinces, Amorites appear in the records by the hundred, food runs short under Ibbi-Sin until Elam sacks Ur about 2004 BC, and in Egypt Mentuhotep II reunites the country by war about 2033 BC.
src: Wikipedia, First Intermediate Period of Egypt

centuries.life: Assur’s merchants run the first long-distance family firms. From the karum at Kanesh in central Anatolia they sell woollen cloth woven by their wives in Assur, send the silver home by caravan and write letters on clay; some 23,000 tablets survive from their houses. Women’s letters are warmer than the men’s, which are all business, and in Kanesh a woman named Zizizi lends money. In Egypt, reunited under the Middle Kingdom, bakers now raise bread in tall cones on square hearths.
centuries.food: Barley bread and beer from Assur to Anatolia, with foodstuffs and spices among the caravan goods; in Egypt, emmer bread baked in cones, lentils, onions, fish and fowl.
centuries.smell: The merchant quarter at Kanesh smelled of donkeys and their loads, of bales of wool and of the clay of letters being written and sealed.
centuries.trouble: Trade and its rules: goods inside the karum go untaxed while they stay there, and families rather than the state carry the risk, while Egypt’s new kings rebuild the crown’s power after a century of division.
src: Wikipedia, First Intermediate Period of Egypt

centuries.life: In the Luoyang basin Erlitou grows into a city of perhaps 24,000, with a palace quarter of twelve hectares inside rammed-earth walls and a bronze foundry run by its lords, the first in China to cast ritual vessels at scale; the ruts of its carts are the oldest in the country. On the Indus the great cities begin to empty from about 1900 BC as the land dries and people move east; the last skeletons show more violence and more disease.
centuries.food: Millet in northern China, as porridge and even as noodles, like the millet noodles more than 4,000 years old found at Lajia in Qinghai; wheat, barley, rice and millets on the Indus.
centuries.smell: Erlitou smelled of the foundry south of the palace, of copper brought from the Zhongtiao mountains being melted, and of rammed earth pounded for new walls.
centuries.trouble: Who holds the sacred bronze: Erlitou’s elite keeps the casting of ritual vessels to itself, and whether its kings were the Xia of later legend is still argued; on the Indus the question is how to live when the rivers fail.

centuries.life: Hammurabi of Babylon conquers his neighbours and, about 1753 BC, sets up a basalt stele 2.25 metres tall carved with laws that run to number 282. They sort people into the awilum, the lesser muskenum and the slave, and price every wrong: a surgeon earns ten shekels of silver for a successful operation with a bronze lancet and loses his hand if the patient dies; a builder whose house falls and kills its owner pays with his life. Boats, wagons, beasts and seasonal labourers all have fixed rates of hire.
centuries.food: Barley bread and beer for most; written down about 1730 BC, the oldest recipes known: 25 stews, most of them of meat such as lamb, cooked with fat, leek, garlic, onion, cumin, coriander, beer, milk or blood.
centuries.smell: A Babylonian kitchen smelled of garlic, leek and onion, of cumin and coriander, and of fat rendering in the stew pot.
centuries.trouble: Justice by rank: an eye for an eye between equals, cheaper lives and smaller fines for the muskenum, and the slave as property, all set in stone by a conqueror who wants every subject to know the price.

centuries.life: On Crete the Minoan palaces are at their height. Knossos, with perhaps 20,000 to 100,000 people, is built round an open court, with red-painted wooden columns, light wells and great storerooms where the palace gathers the farms’ grain, oil and wine and gives them out again. Town houses rise two or three storeys, stone below and mud brick above, on paved and drained streets. Up the Nile, Kerma, Egypt’s rival in Nubia, has become a city of 25 hectares round the mudbrick temple of the Western Deffufa.
centuries.food: Wheat, barley, chickpeas, grapes, figs and olive oil, the main cooking fat, with mutton, pork, goat and some fish on Crete; bread and the beef of great herds at Kerma.
centuries.smell: A Minoan town smelled of olive oil and of wine made in the palace workshops, of sheep’s wool, the island’s cloth, and of the sea.
centuries.trouble: Who gathers the surplus and who gives it out: the palaces of Crete and Nubia hold the stores, and the kings of Kerma, buried with thousands of cattle skulls and many sacrificed people, grow strong enough to challenge Egypt.

centuries.life: Around 1600 BC Thera blows apart in an eruption of the seventh magnitude, throwing out tens of cubic kilometres of rock; Akrotiri, warned by months of earthquakes, empties before the pumice buries it, and tsunamis strike the north coast of Crete. Egypt is divided: a dynasty of Levantine origin rules the Delta from Avaris, Thebes holds the south, and Kerma’s army raids deep into Upper Egypt. In China a later chronicle remembers yellow fog, a dim sun, frost in July and famine as the Xia gave way to the Shang.
centuries.food: Bread, olive oil, figs and wine in the Aegean, from fields ploughed with donkeys and oxen; along the Nile, bakers of the new kingdom slap their dough onto the hot inner walls of cylindrical clay ovens.
centuries.smell: Thera smelled of sulphur in the months of warning, before the ash and pumice came down over Akrotiri.
centuries.trouble: Who will unite the Nile: Kamose and then Ahmose I of Thebes fight the kings of Avaris, intercept their letters to Kerma, and by about 1550 BC the Delta is Egyptian again.

centuries.life: Egypt has annexed Nubia, and its kings are buried in the Valley of the Kings by a village of craftsmen. At Deir el-Medina some 68 mudbrick houses on stone footings, four or five rooms each, line one narrow street; the men work in two gangs, eight days on and two off, and the tomb scribe notes why they stay away: illness, a quarrel with a wife, a hangover. Many villagers, women too, can read. On Crete, about 1450 BC, Greek-speaking Mycenaean lords take over Knossos.
centuries.food: Rations of grain, up to three times a field hand’s, made into bread by the wives and into beer brewed under the eye of the mistress of the house; an Egyptian labourer’s pay was about five and a half sacks of grain a month.
centuries.smell: Deir el-Medina smelled of bread and brewing, of water carried up from a well half an hour’s walk away, and of stone dust from the royal tombs.
centuries.trouble: Empire and its price: Egypt destroys Kerma and rules Nubia, the Nubians rebel for two centuries, and on Crete the palaces burn about 1470 BC before a Mycenaean elite takes Knossos.

centuries.life: The great kings of the Near East write to one another in Akkadian, and more than 300 of their clay letters turn up at Amarna, the city Akhenaten builds in haste about 1346 BC of whitewashed mud brick for his one god, the Aten, and which is abandoned soon after his death. In Greece the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos and Knossos keep Linear B accounts of land, rations and labour; the Knossos tablets count some 80,000 to 100,000 sheep, and women in palace workgroups weave the wool.
centuries.food: Bread, beer, onions and fish along the Nile; in Greece, cereal given out by the palaces for festivals and communal meals, with olive oil, the chief export, and wine.
centuries.smell: A Mycenaean palace smelled of perfumed oil, which its scribes watched as closely as bronze, and of the wool of its flocks; Akhetaten of fresh whitewash on mud brick.
centuries.trouble: Faith and power: Akhenaten builds a city for one god, yet people there keep images of Bes, Taweret and Isis, and after him the court returns to Thebes and the old gods; in Greece the common people owe labour and taxes to the palace.

centuries.life: On the Huan river at Anyang the late Shang kings build a capital of some 25 square kilometres, a hundred times larger than any other site on the North China Plain, with rammed-earth halls and workshops for bronze and bone. Diviners crack turtle shells and ox shoulder blades and write question and answer on the bone: planting, wind and rain, war, childbirth. Commoners owe the king labour, not goods, and at least 14,197 human victims, half of them Qiang captives, are named in the inscriptions as sacrificed.
centuries.food: Foxtail and broomcorn millet, the staple, and an ale of fermented millet poured from bronze jue for the great and from clay copies for the lesser; cattle, sheep, pigs and dogs went to the ancestors and then, probably, to the lords’ feasts.
centuries.smell: Anyang smelled of its bronze and bone workshops, of the scorched shell and bone of the diviners, and of the blood of sacrifice.
centuries.trouble: What the ancestors want: the kings ask them about every harvest and campaign and pay them in people and cattle, a thousand cattle in a single rite, while Fu Hao, queen and general, leads armies against the neighbours.

centuries.life: Within a few decades after 1200 BC the palace world of the eastern Mediterranean breaks. Mycenae burns about 1190 BC and Pylos about 1180; Ugarit falls by 1178, its last king writing that enemy ships have come while his own are away. Ramesses III beats back the Sea Peoples but empties his treasury. At Deir el-Medina, in his 29th year, the royal tomb-builders, eighteen days into a month without rations, lay down their tools and sit in at the temples: the first strike on record.
centuries.food: Grain was both wage and grievance: the strikers demanded grain, meat, oil and vegetables, and in one month received two bushels of emmer.
centuries.smell: The Levantine coast smelled of burning cities, as Ugarit and Emar went up in flames between about 1187 and 1175 BC.
centuries.trouble: Hunger, raiders and the failure of kings: drought in Anatolia, perhaps plague and the raids of the Sea Peoples strain every state at once, and in Greece writing itself is lost for four centuries.

centuries.life: On the Gulf coast of Mexico the Olmec lords of San Lorenzo carve colossal heads, ten of them here, from basalt dragged from the Tuxtla mountains; moving one took perhaps 1,500 people three or four months. Most people live in villages on higher ground, each house with a lean-to and storage pits, planting the river banks between floods and clearing new fields with fire. They play a ballgame with balls of rubber. In China, about 1046 BC, the Zhou overthrow the last Shang king at Muye.
centuries.food: Maize, beans, squash, cassava and sweet potato, with fish, turtles, deer and, at San Lorenzo, dog, the commonest meat of all; avocado and cacao probably grew beside the houses.
centuries.smell: An Olmec village smelled of fields burned for planting, of river mud after the floods and of latex being worked into rubber.
centuries.trouble: Who commands the water and the stone: an Olmec elite controls the rivers, the jade from Guatemala and the labour to move its monuments, though there is no sign of a standing army.

centuries.life: In the Wei valley the Zhou kings rule through kinsmen planted in colonies across the plain, and record each appointment and campaign in long inscriptions cast inside bronze vessels; human sacrifice, so common under the Shang, has stopped. On the Ganges plain the Vedic tribes are turning from cattle to the plough: iron axes and ploughs spread after 1000 BC, wheat, rice and barley go into big storage jars, and cattle are still the measure of wealth. Women milk, card wool, weave and grind the grain.
centuries.food: Milk and dairy, grains, fruit and vegetables on the Ganges, with meat but not the cow, and the drinks soma and sura; millet, meat and ale at the Zhou ancestral feasts.
centuries.smell: A Vedic village smelled of cattle and milk, of the dyer’s vats and of grain stored in jars; a Zhou hall of millet ale and meat at the feasts for the ancestors.
centuries.trouble: Who may rule: the Zhou claim the favour of Tian, heaven, for their conquest, while in India the rajan answers to the councils of the sabha and samiti and a hierarchy of varna begins to set.

centuries.life: Assyria makes war a yearly business. Ashurnasirpal II builds Kalhu, at Nimrud, as his new capital: walls 7.5 kilometres long round 360 hectares, a palace guarded by winged, man-headed lions, and gardens and a zoo stocked from his campaigns. Governors, deputies and village managers collect the taxes in labour and in goods. In Greece, emerging from its dark age, only four places hold more than a thousand people, and by 900 BC almost every weapon laid in a grave is of iron.
centuries.food: For the ten-day feast that opened Kalhu in 864 BC, 69,574 guests, 16,000 of them townspeople, got through 10,000 pigeons, 10,000 jugs of beer and 10,000 skins of wine, among countless other things.
centuries.smell: Kalhu smelled of new mud brick, of beer and wine for the king’s feasts, and of the botanical garden and zoo filled with the plants and beasts of conquered lands.
centuries.trouble: Tribute or ruin: the Assyrian army marches out to collect, with cavalry and siege engines for those who refuse, and by the next century whole peoples are deported by the tens of thousands.

centuries.life: Greece comes out of its dark age with the Phoenician alphabet, to which it adds vowels, and with more people: the population roughly doubles in the eighth century and villages merge into cities, Athens growing from perhaps 1,500 people towards 5,000. In Sicily and southern Italy a new Greek town is founded about every other year, and the first Olympic games are held in 776 BC. Houses average 45 to 50 square metres, and barely half of children live to eighteen.
centuries.food: Barley or the preferred wheat, pulses, fruit and vegetables from small, mixed farms, olives and grapes for oil and wine to sell, and sheep and goats for milk, wool and meat.
centuries.smell: A Greek village smelled of olive oil and new wine, of sheep and goats folded near the houses, and of their dung carried out to the fields.
centuries.trouble: Land and debt, as people multiply and the work falls to slaves, sharecroppers and debtors; in China the Zhou capital is sacked in 771 BC and the court flees east, and on the Nile Piye of Kush takes Lower Egypt about 727 BC.

centuries.life: Assyria rules by tax, corvée and deportation. Sennacherib rebuilds Nineveh with a wall 12 kilometres long and 25 metres high and a park that may lie behind the legend of the Hanging Gardens; his successors take Memphis in 671 BC and sack Thebes in 663, driving the Kushite pharaohs back to Napata. Aramaic, carried by the deported, becomes the common tongue of the region. In Lydia, about 650 BC, the first coins are struck, and in Greece armoured hoplites fight in close ranks.
centuries.food: Bread, beer and wine in Assyria, where village managers take part of every harvest as tax; wheat or barley, pulses, olive oil and wine in Greece.
centuries.smell: Nineveh smelled of new brick and the king’s great park; far up the Nile, Meroë smelled of iron bloomeries, whose fuel stripped the Butana plain of its forests and left heaps of slag.
centuries.trouble: Empire and resistance: Judah, aided by Kush, defies Sennacherib in 701 BC, and in 612 the Medes and Babylonians take Nineveh after a two-month siege and loot it; in Greek cities tyrants such as Cypselus of Corinth take power from the nobles.

centuries.life: On the Ganges plain India builds its first great cities since the Indus: sixteen kingdoms and republics from Gandhara to Anga, with Kashi at Varanasi, Kausambi a trading town and Magadha rising. Wandering teachers challenge the Vedic priests, and Buddhism and Jainism are born. In Athens, Solon, made mediator in 594 BC, ends slavery for debt and makes income, not birth, the test for office. Cyrus founds the Persian empire; by 500 BC it may hold 17 to 35 million people.
centuries.food: Rice, wheat, barley and milk on the Ganges plain; barley or wheat, olive oil, pulses and wine in Greece; and in Persia grain as tribute, 120,000 measures a year from Egypt alone.
centuries.smell: An Indian market town smelled of cattle and milk, of leather and dye, and of the potter’s kiln.
centuries.trouble: Debt and who counts as a citizen: Athens’ poor work off their debts as bondsmen until Solon ends it, India’s new kingdoms swallow its republics, and Persia makes the whole Near East one tribute-paying state.

centuries.life: Athens at its height may hold 250,000 to 300,000 people. When the Spartans invade in 431 BC, the farmers of Attica crowd inside the Long Walls, tripling the numbers there, and in 430 a plague kills 75,000 to 100,000, about a quarter of the people; the sick die alone and the temples fill with corpses. In Persia, Darius’s scribes at Persepolis write more than 10,000 tablets on the empire’s stores, and couriers ride the 2,500-kilometre Royal Road in fifteen days.
centuries.food: Wheat or barley, olive oil, pulses and wine in Greece; in Persia, tribute in kind fed court and army, Babylon alone sending four months’ food for the army each year.
centuries.smell: Athens in the plague years smelled of the dead, heaped together in the streets and temples or thrown onto pyres already burning.
centuries.trouble: Who leads the Greeks: Athens and Sparta go to war in 431 BC, and inside the walls the plague breaks law and piety, as the rich die and their wealth passes to poorer kin.

centuries.life: In China the state of Qin remakes its people for farming and war. From 356 BC Shang Yang’s laws punish anyone who knows of a crime and fails to report it as harshly as the criminal, reward farmers who beat their harvest quotas, tax twice the households that keep several grown sons under one roof, and rank soldiers in twenty grades by what they achieve in battle. Alexander marches from Macedon in 334 BC with about 48,000 men, founds more than twenty cities and dies at Babylon in 323.
centuries.food: Wheat or barley, olive oil, pulses and wine in the Greek world that Alexander carries east; on Qin’s farms the harvest itself was the test, rewarded above the quota and punished below it.
centuries.smell: An army on Alexander’s road smelled of some 48,000 men and 6,100 horses, a moving city that marched for ten years from Macedon to the Indus and back to Babylon.
centuries.trouble: How to rule many peoples: Alexander marries his officers to Persian noblewomen at Susa and gives Persians commands, to his own soldiers’ anger, while in India the Nanda kings of Magadha swallow the old kingdoms from about 345 BC and in Qin the law reaches into every household.

centuries.life: India is one empire for the first time. From Pataliputra, behind a wooden wall with 64 gates and 570 towers, the Mauryas count their subjects by trade and claim all the land, giving seed, tools and grain reserves in return for tribute. After the Kalinga war of 261 BC kills some 100,000 people, Ashoka turns to the Buddha’s teaching and has wells dug, trees planted along the roads and medicine given to people and animals. In Kush the kings now go to their pyramids at Meroë.
centuries.food: The grain of the fertile eastern Ganges plain, held in royal reserves against hard years, and under Ashoka an edict against killing wild animals.
centuries.smell: Pataliputra smelled of wood smoke and timber, a city walled in wood, and of the cargoes of the river trade; Meroë smelled of its iron furnaces.
centuries.trouble: War and conscience: after Kalinga, Ashoka’s edicts preach restraint across India while thirty commissioners in the capital regulate wages, trade and sales taxes, and occupations harden into castes.

centuries.life: The Han rule China for four centuries. Small landowning farmers rank just below scholars and officials; tenants, labourers and slaves come lower, and registered merchants must wear white and pay heavy taxes. Families of four or five live together, and men are called up at 23 for a year’s training and a year’s service. Zhang Qian’s journeys west, 139 to 125 BC, open the road that becomes the Silk Road. In Rome, Tiberius Gracchus is killed in 133 BC for giving public land to the poor.
centuries.food: Wheat, barley, millet, rice and beans, with pork, poultry, mutton, fish and game, seasoned with soy sauce, salt, honey and sugar, washed down with beer and yellow wine; from the west came sesame, peas, onions, coriander and cucumber.
centuries.smell: A Han county town smelled of the state’s iron works and salt, of pigs, ducks and geese, and of beer and yellow wine.
centuries.trouble: Who owns the land and who works it: in Italy great estates worked by slaves push the Gracchi to land reform and Sicily’s slaves to revolt in 138 BC, while in China the state takes salt and iron into its own hands in 117 BC.

centuries.life: Rome rules the Mediterranean and cannot govern itself. The Social War of 91 to 87 BC triples the number of citizens; Sulla’s soldiers kill for profit and his lists make murder legal. In 73 BC some seventy gladiators break out of a school near Capua, and Spartacus leads an army of about 70,000; when Crassus wins, 6,000 are crucified along the Appian Way. From 58 BC the citizens of Rome get their grain free. In Mexico the first buildings of Teotihuacan rise; in Nubia, Kandake Amanirenas fights Roman Egypt.
centuries.food: Free grain for the citizens of Rome from 58 BC, made into bread and porridge, with olive oil, wine and garum, the fermented fish sauce traded across the sea.
centuries.smell: In 71 BC the Appian Way smelled of death for more than a hundred miles, where 6,000 of Spartacus’ followers hung on crosses between Capua and Rome.
centuries.trouble: Land, citizenship and the army: the Italian allies fight Rome for the vote, generals turn their legions on the city, and Caesar crosses the Rubicon in 49 BC and is killed in 44.

centuries.life: Under Augustus the Roman Empire holds some 55 to 60 million people, a sixth to a quarter of the world. In Italy one person in four or five is a slave; the top one and a half per cent of households take a fifth of all income, and the great majority live near subsistence. Inscriptions in Rome name 268 trades, and enslaved men and women in the city die, on average, at about seventeen. In Mexico the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan nears completion, 65 metres high.
centuries.food: Bread from shipped grain, the empire’s chief cargo, with olive oil, wine and garum, the fermented fish sauce sold in jars across the empire.
centuries.smell: A Roman town smelled of garum and olive oil in the shops, of wine, and of the crowds and furnaces of the public baths.
centuries.trouble: Who shares the peace: a near-subsistence majority under a tiny rich elite, slaves freed so often that a law of 2 BC limits how many an owner may free in his will, and freedmen rising so high in the emperor’s service that Hadrian will curb them.

centuries.life: At Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico the Pyramid of the Sun is finished by about AD 100, and the city fills with some 2,000 walled apartment compounds of 60 to 100 people each, with whole neighbourhoods of migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf coast and obsidian workshops that make the city rich. In the Roman Empire a plague that seems to start at the siege of Seleucia in 165 kills perhaps 5 to 10 million, about one in ten; Marcus Aurelius fills the ranks with gladiators, slaves and bandits.
centuries.food: Maize, beans, amaranth, tomatillos and pumpkins at Teotihuacan; in Han China, wheat, barley, millet, rice and beans, with pork and poultry, soy sauce and yellow wine.
centuries.smell: Teotihuacan smelled of cooking fires in thousands of apartment courtyards and of the textiles and pottery made in its neighbourhood workshops.
centuries.trouble: In China the Yellow Turbans rise across eight provinces in 184 and are crushed within a year; in Rome the plague empties the legions just as Germanic invaders break in, driven out only by 171.

centuries.life: The Roman world nearly breaks. Between 235 and 284 at least 26 men claim the throne, the silver coinage is debased with bronze and copper until prices run away, and some taxes are taken in kind. A plague from about 251 to 262 is said to cut the people of Alexandria by 62 per cent. Cities shrink and build thick walls, Rome among them; townspeople move out to the land, and small farmers bind themselves to great estates as coloni. In China the Han fall in 220.
centuries.food: Bread, oil and wine, more and more from the estate one lived on, as trade broke down and landowners turned to subsistence farming and barter.
centuries.smell: A Roman town smelled of lime and mortar from the thick new walls going up round its shrinking streets.
centuries.trouble: Who can hold the empire together: Gaul and Britain break away under their own emperors from 260, Zenobia of Palmyra takes Syria and Egypt, and Aurelian wins them back by 274.
src: Wikipedia, Crisis of the Third Century

centuries.life: The Roman Empire survives by taxing harder. Diocletian’s army is said to have counted 389,704 men and his fleets 45,562; gold buys two and a half times as much as it did in 274, a sign of a gold-rich elite over a cash-poor peasantry. In Armorica almost every villa is deserted by 350, and money stops changing hands there about 360. In 376 Goths fleeing the Huns cross the Danube, and in 378 they destroy an eastern army at Adrianople. In India the Guptas rise from about 320.
centuries.food: In the Roman West, what the farm grew rather than what the market sold, as the villas emptied and coin went out of use; in India, pepper among the luxuries shipped west with silk, ivory and pearls.
centuries.smell: A fort on the Rhine smelled of the plough and the byre, its soldiers now paid in land rather than wages.
centuries.trouble: Who carries the cost of defence: heavy taxes ruin trades and city councils lose their revenues, and by 400 Armorica is held not by the emperor but by the bagaudae.
src: Wikipedia, Fall of the Western Roman Empire

centuries.life: The Western Empire comes apart. In 405 and 406 perhaps 100,000 Germanic and Alan people cross the Rhine; Alaric’s siege starves Rome, which in 410 is sacked for three days, the first time an enemy has taken it in eight centuries, and in 476 Odoacer sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople. In Gupta India the Chinese monk Faxian, travelling between 405 and 411, finds offences punished by fines rather than death and no register of households. Teotihuacan holds perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 people.
centuries.food: In Gupta India, Faxian found, people killed no living creature, drank no intoxicants and ate no onions or garlic; in southern China tea was now drunk; in Rome, under siege from 408 to 410, there was famine.
centuries.smell: A late Roman town smelled more of the farmyard and less of the bath-house, as its council lost its revenues and let its public services lapse.
centuries.trouble: Who protects the provinces: the Western army dwindles until Stilicho drafts 12,000 prisoners, frontier land is given up to the Germans, and from the late fifth century the Huns break into India.
src: Wikipedia, Fall of the Western Roman Empire

centuries.life: In 541 plague comes to Constantinople on the grain ships from Egypt and may kill 40 per cent of the city, up to 5,000 a day at its height by modern estimates. Tax revenues fall as farms empty, landowners are made to pay the tax on their dead neighbours’ fields, and in Egypt wages rise by up to 150 per cent. In Mexico, about 550, Teotihuacan’s palaces are sacked and burned after drought; in India the last Gupta kings give way to the Huns.
centuries.food: Egyptian grain, the bread of Constantinople, carried in the same ships that carried the plague; in southern China, tea, drunk there since the fifth century.
centuries.smell: Constantinople in 542 smelled of the unburied dead, stacked in the open because there was no room left to bury them.
centuries.trouble: Who pays when people die: the Eastern Empire squeezes the survivors for the taxes of the dead, while the burning of Teotihuacan, aimed mostly at the rulers’ buildings, may have been a revolt from within.

centuries.life: In 609 a census counts about 50 million people in China, and from 618 the Tang rule them from Chang’an, a walled grid more than ten kilometres across, cut into 108 walled wards with four gates each and two supervised markets. Each family is allotted a nominal 100 mu of land and owes grain, cloth and labour. In Arabia, a man of the Quraysh of Mecca, Muhammad, begins to preach about 613, leaves for Medina in 622 and, with 10,000 followers, takes Mecca in 630.
centuries.food: Barley, garlic, turnips, soybeans, pears, peaches, jujubes and pomegranates in Tang China, with pork, chicken and, in the north, lamb; in Arabia, the dates of oases such as Khaybar and Fadak.
centuries.smell: Chang’an smelled of the goods of its two great markets and of the dust of its avenues; Mecca, of camels and the caravans loading for Syria.
centuries.trouble: Faith and clan: the Quraysh boycott Muhammad’s clan from about 616 to 619, the Constitution of Medina binds Arab and Jewish tribes to defend the oasis together, and in China the rich begin to buy up the land the equal-field system was meant to share.

centuries.life: In 762 the Abbasids found Baghdad, a round walled city with four gates, built by a workforce of 100,000; by 794 it has a paper mill, and soon it is known for its bookshops. Christians and Jews keep their faith and pay the jizya, and an elite household may own a thousand slaves. In China the An Lushan rebellion of 755 to 763 ends the Tang golden age, and in 780 the old taxes in grain, cloth and labour give way to a cash tax paid twice a year.
centuries.food: In Chang’an, for those who could pay, golden peaches from Samarkand, pistachios and figs from Persia and mangoes from the south, and sugar from cane, learned from India in the seventh century; from Baghdad’s world, sugar, almonds and citrus travel west to Spain.
centuries.smell: Baghdad smelled of its new trades: sugar boiling, rope and matting, silk and textiles, and the paper mill of 794.
centuries.trouble: Who belongs: non-Arab Muslims push into the elite and non-Muslims pay their tax as protected subjects, while in China the rebellion breaks the dynasty’s hold on its own provinces.

centuries.life: Since the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, the Northmen are at sea. At home they live on farms of free karls under the jarls, with thralls, as much as a quarter of the people, doing the hardest work; captives are sold east for Arab silver, and Iceland is settled. In the Maya lowlands Tikal, Copán and Calakmul fall silent: dated monuments drop from about forty a year around 750 to none by 900, as the rains fail by up to half. In Iraq the enslaved Zanj rise in 869.
centuries.food: Porridge and bread of barley and wheat, meat cured, smoked or made into sausages, cod, salmon, herring and seal, skyr, butter and cheese, beer and mead; the poor man’s bread was gritty from the quern and full of weed seeds.
centuries.smell: A Norse farm smelled of meat curing in the smoke, of herring and seal, of butter and skyr, and of beer and mead.
centuries.trouble: Raid, trade and slavery: weapon injuries scar 72 per cent of the examined men of Viking Age Norway and 42 per cent of the women, slaves go east for silver, and in the Maya south the divine kings lose their hold as the rain fails.

centuries.life: The Rus’ princes of Kiev ride out each year on the poliudie to gather tribute in money, furs or slaves, and send furs, beeswax, honey and slaves down the Dnieper on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks. Most of their five million or so subjects grow grain and keep livestock. In 988 Vladimir orders Kiev baptised. In the Yucatán the northern cities of Chichén Itzá and Uxmal carry on after the south has emptied, and the Copán valley holds 15,000 people, about half its peak.
centuries.food: Cereal porridge and bread with the meat and milk of their beasts, and honey, which the Rus’ also sold south to Constantinople.
centuries.smell: Kiev smelled of furs, beeswax and honey stacked for the river convoys to Constantinople.
centuries.trouble: Old gods or new: Vladimir’s baptism of Kiev meets its fiercest resistance in the northern towns of Novgorod, Suzdal and Belozersk.

centuries.life: Song China counts 20 million households, perhaps 90 million people. Its furnaces make more than 100,000 tonnes of iron a year, now on coal instead of charcoal; its mints strike some six billion copper coins in 1085, and the state prints the first government paper money. From 1011 a drought-proof rice from Champa gives two harvests a year. On the Mississippi, Cahokia rises about 1050 round a plaza of 50 acres. In Egypt the Nile fails, and Fustat empties in seven years of famine.
centuries.food: Rice in the south, two crops a year from Champa seed, with pork and salted fish for the poor; in Cairo in the famine of 1064 to 1071, dogs sold for five silver dirhams each until there were none left.
centuries.smell: Kaifeng smelled of coal, which the iron works now burned instead of charcoal, and of restaurants serving southern food to officials far from home.
centuries.trouble: Who rises and who starves: some 30,000 candidates a year sit the Song prefectural examinations, while in Egypt rival slave regiments of Turks and Sudanese fight over a weak caliph as some 40,000 people die of hunger.

centuries.life: In 1127 the Jurchen take Kaifeng with two emperors and most of the court, and the Song rebuild south of the Yangtze at Hangzhou, which grows from about 200,000 people to 500,000 by 1170; its paper-money works employ more than a thousand people a day. On the Mississippi, Cahokia is at its height, 15,000 or more in pole-and-thatch houses round Monks Mound, thirty metres of heaped earth; about 1175 it builds a palisade three kilometres long. By 1200 Kiev is about the size of Paris, and London has some 30,000.
centuries.food: In Hangzhou, breakfast sellers on the Imperial Way offer tripe, mutton, goose, soups and pancakes, and the noodle shops never close; at Cahokia, maize alongside the old seed crops, goosefoot and sumpweed.
centuries.smell: Hangzhou smelled of noodle shops open day and night and of night markets that shut at the third watch and opened again at the fifth; Cahokia, of thatch, wood smoke and the earth heaped onto its mounds.
centuries.trouble: Walls and war: the Song fight the Jurchen for the north, and Cahokia, once open, shuts itself behind a palisade that it rebuilds smaller and smaller as people leave.

centuries.life: From 1206 the Mongols of Genghis Khan ride out, each soldier with five or six horses, sparing the cities that surrender and massacring those that resist, all but the craftsmen. Kiev falls in 1240, and Baghdad is sacked in 1258. Then comes a hard peace: merchants with papers travel under protection, and under Kublai some 1,400 relay stations with 50,000 horses carry messages 200 kilometres a day. Hangzhou passes a million people, and 400,000 candidates a year sit the Song examinations.
centuries.food: In Hangzhou the poor ate rice, pork and salted fish and the rich deer, hare, pheasant, quail and shellfish, rice wine was commoner than grape, and eleven kinds of apricot and eight of pear came to market.
centuries.smell: A Mongol relay station smelled of horses, oxen and mules by the thousand, kept ready every forty kilometres along the roads of the empire.
centuries.trouble: Conquest and tolerance: the Mongols massacre whole cities, yet decree freedom of religion, spare the poor and the clergy from tax and, from 1252, count every subject for a fixed poll tax.

centuries.life: Between 1346 and 1353 plague runs from the Crimea through Constantinople and Sicily to every corner of Europe and the Middle East, killing perhaps 30 to 60 per cent of Europeans and a third of the people of the Middle East. Half of Paris dies; Florence falls from some 120,000 people to 50,000; Cairo, with up to 600,000, loses more than a third in eight months. Earlier, in 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali had crossed Cairo on his way to Mecca with, later chroniclers said, eighty camels carrying gold.
centuries.food: In Yuan China Hu Sihui compiles the Yinshan Zhengyao, a guide to food and health that joins Mongol and Chinese cooking, and sorghum arrives from the west; in Mali the kings grow rich taxing the trade in salt and gold.
centuries.smell: Europe smelled of the plague pits, dug because there were too many dead for the churchyards, some holding hundreds or thousands of bodies; the doctors of Paris blamed a pestilence in the air.
centuries.trouble: Whom to blame: Jewish communities are attacked and destroyed, lepers too, while Ragusa invents quarantine in 1377 and wages, rents and taxes are thrown into disorder.

centuries.life: Tenochtitlan, on its island in Lake Texcoco, holds more than 200,000 people in four quarters of twenty districts each; commoners live in reed houses plastered with mud, most people bathe twice a day, and 20,000 or more trade daily at the Tlatelolco market. In the Andes the Inca, from 1438, rule perhaps ten million people without money or markets: each household owes the state labour, and storehouses stand a day’s walk apart. In Mainz, about 1440, Gutenberg begins to print; by 1500 Europe’s presses have made 20 million copies.
centuries.food: Potatoes of more than 200 kinds and chuño, potato freeze-dried, with maize beer, and coca leaves to ease hunger at work in the Andes; in Tenochtitlan, the harvest of the chinampa fields built out into the lake.
centuries.smell: Tenochtitlan smelled of its canals and canoes and of the spring water carried in from Chapultepec by two terracotta aqueducts; Constantinople in 1453 smelled of the powder of Orban’s great bombard.
centuries.trouble: Empire and faith: the Ottomans take Constantinople in 1453 with 50,000 to 80,000 men against 7,000 defenders and enslave perhaps 30,000 of its people, while the Inca move whole colonies of subjects across the Andes.

centuries.life: The oceans join the world, and the Americas pay. Smallpox appears there in 1518; in 1520 it kills perhaps 40 per cent of Tenochtitlan’s 200,000 people, and over the century Mexico falls from an estimated 20 million to barely more than one. At Potosí, founded in 1545 on a mountain of silver, Spain drafts some 13,000 Andean men a year into mines that yield 60 per cent of the world’s silver. In Germany, printers sell 300,000 copies of Luther’s writings between 1518 and 1520.
centuries.food: New crops cross the oceans: maize and sweet potatoes to China, where the sweet potato, arriving about 1560, becomes the food of the poor, cassava to Africa and tomatoes to Spain, while wheat, sugar cane, cattle, pigs and horses go west.
centuries.smell: Potosí smelled of mercury, used from 1554 to draw the silver out of the ore, and of the coca leaves that women sold in its street markets.
centuries.trouble: Who owns the New World and its people: Spain conquers, the forced labour of the mita feeds the silver mines, and in Europe Luther’s printed pamphlets split the Church.

centuries.life: The world is cold. European winters run more than a degree below the twentieth-century average, the Thames freezes for frost fairs from 1608, and in the Swiss Alps advancing glaciers crush farms and villages. The Thirty Years’ War, 1618 to 1648, leaves some regions of the Holy Roman Empire with 70 per cent fewer people. In north China drought and floods sap the Ming until rebels enter Beijing in 1644. In 1696 and 1697 famine kills a fifth of the people of Estonia and a third of Finland.
centuries.food: When the harvests failed, Alpine villagers ate bread of ground nutshells mixed with barley and oat flour; in England, sugar from the slave plantations of the Caribbean turned from luxury to habit, from one pound a head a year in 1670 towards twenty-five a century later.
centuries.smell: London in the winter of 1684, the coldest on record, smelled of the frost fair’s booths and braziers on the frozen Thames.
centuries.trouble: Cold, hunger and fear: as the climate worsens, wars, revolts and witch trials multiply, the accused mostly poor women and widows, blamed for late frosts, cattle plague and disease.

centuries.life: The Atlantic slave trade reaches its height in the last two decades of the century; in all some 12.75 million Africans are loaded onto ships, held for months below deck, and up to two million die at sea. Dahomey, Oyo and Asante sell captives for guns, gunpowder, alcohol and Indian cloth. In London three children in four born in the 1730s and 1740s die before the age of five, but the cotton mills multiply: Britain spins 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton in 1750 and 52 million in 1800.
centuries.food: Sugar, coffee, tea and chocolate, grown by enslaved hands, become everyday pleasures in Europe; the English eat 25 pounds of sugar a head a year by 1770, up from one in 1670.
centuries.smell: A slave ship smelled of hundreds of captives held for months in tight, unsanitary holds, with nets rigged along the sides to catch those who jumped.
centuries.trouble: Freedom and its price: Britain bans its slave trade only in 1807, while the new mills set orphans and children as young as eight to work twelve to fourteen hours a day.

centuries.life: Steam and coal pull people into towns. Manchester’s population rises sixfold between 1771 and 1831, Bradford’s by half every ten years, London’s from under a million to three million. Newcomers crowd into slums with dirt floors and no sanitation, sewage runs raw into the rivers, and cholera kills 14,137 Londoners in 1848 and 1849. Yet the share of London children dying before five has fallen to a third. After the Great Stink of 1858, London digs 82 miles of main sewers.
centuries.food: Bread kept dear by the Corn Laws until 1846, chronic hunger for many until late in the century, and tea, coffee, sugar, tobacco and chocolate now within reach of ordinary Europeans.
centuries.smell: London in the hot summer of 1858 smelled of the Thames, thick with sewage, so badly that Parliament soaked its curtains in chloride of lime.
centuries.trouble: Who shares the wealth of the machines: wages rise slowly, by some estimates only 15 per cent between the 1780s and the 1850s, labourers smash threshing machines in the Swing Riots of 1830, and slavery lasts in Cuba until 1886.

centuries.life: Two world wars bracket most lives. The first, 1914 to 1918, kills 15 to 22 million; on 1 July 1916 the British lose 19,200 dead on the Somme in one day, and four empires fall. In 1918 influenza infects 500 million, a third of humanity, and kills 25 to 50 million, 12 to 17 million of them in India. The Depression puts a quarter of Americans out of work by 1933. The second war kills 60 to 75 million, and in 1947 Partition uproots 12 to 20 million in India.
centuries.food: In the Depression families made do with soups, beans, noodles and the cheapest cuts, sometimes horse meat, stretching the Sunday roast into sandwiches and soup; in the 1918 epidemic some shops made customers leave their orders outside.
centuries.smell: The Western Front smelled of a trench line from the Channel to Switzerland, where lice, trench foot, typhus and trench fever bred in the mud.
centuries.trouble: Class, nation and empire: the Bolsheviks take Russia in 1917, crop prices fall by up to 60 per cent and a third of American farmers lose their land, Hitler becomes chancellor in 1933, and India and Pakistan divide in 1947.

centuries.life: Polio comes back every summer: the United States records nearly 58,000 cases in 1952, and children breathe in iron lungs until Salk’s vaccine is announced in April 1955 and Sabin’s oral vaccine is licensed in 1962. Ghana wins its independence in 1957 and Algeria in 1962. In China the Great Leap Forward and its grain requisitions bring a famine, 1959 to 1961, that kills perhaps 30 to 46 million. From 1975 nearly 800,000 Vietnamese escape by boat. In 1981 American doctors first recognise AIDS.
centuries.food: As people move to the cities, diets shift from grains, fruit and vegetables to processed food richer in meat, sugar, refined flour and fat; in China in the famine years, people ate soil.
centuries.smell: A port smelled of ships’ diesel as the shipping container, invented in 1956, cut the cost of carrying goods round the world.
centuries.trouble: Freedom and its terms: colonies become states, pirates attack 349 of the 452 refugee boats that reach Thailand in 1981, and AIDS brings stigma as well as death.

centuries.life: In 2007, for the first time, more than half of humanity lives in cities, and by 2026 three people in four have used the internet; at any moment about half a million are in the air. Then, from Wuhan at the end of 2019, a new coronavirus: by April 2020 some 3.9 billion people, more than half the world, are under some form of lockdown, offices empty and schools close. More than 7 million deaths are confirmed, and the excess dead are put at 18 to 35 million.
centuries.food: City diets of processed food richer in meat, sugar, refined grains and fat, with less time to cook and more food ready-made, and body weight and cholesterol rising with income.
centuries.smell: An airport smelled of jet fuel and coffee, with international tourist arrivals passing a billion a year for the first time in 2012.
centuries.trouble: Who gets the benefits: 40.9 million people live with HIV, 32.1 million of them on treatment, 13.7 billion doses of vaccine are given against COVID-19, and the poor are often left out of what globalisation offers.

people.t: Jurist, theologian and Sufi of Tus; his Incoherence of the Philosophers answered Avicenna, and after a crisis in 1095 he left Baghdad to write the Revival of the Religious Sciences. Born c. 1058 and died in Tus on 19 December 1111.
Franciscan logician and nominalist, born c. 1287 at Ockham in Surrey; summoned to Avignon, he fled to the court of Louis of Bavaria in 1328 and died in Munich, probably in April 1347.
Historian of Tunis, born 27 May 1332, whose Muqaddimah, written in six months before 1378, set out a theory of the rise and fall of dynasties; he died in Cairo on 17 March 1406.
Neapolitan philosopher of history, born 23 June 1668, whose New Science of 1725 read the course of nations in their myths and languages; he died in Naples on 23 January 1744.
Irish philosopher and bishop of Cloyne, born 12 March 1685 at Dysart Castle near Thomastown; his Principles of 1710 argued that to be is to be perceived. He died in Oxford on 14 January 1753.

Logician and founder of pragmatism, born 10 September 1839 in Cambridge, Massachusetts; his How to Make Our Ideas Clear of 1878 stated the pragmatic maxim. He died in Milford, Pennsylvania, on 19 April 1914.
Founder of phenomenology, born 8 April 1859 in Prossnitz in Moravia; the Logical Investigations of 1900–01 and the Ideas of 1913 set its method. He died in Freiburg on 27 April 1938.

Philosopher of science, born in Vienna on 28 July 1902; the Logic of Scientific Discovery of 1934 made falsifiability the mark of science and The Open Society of 1945 the case against Plato, Hegel and Marx. He died in London on 17 September 1994.

Political philosopher, born in Baltimore on 21 February 1921; A Theory of Justice of 1971 asked what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance. He died at home in Lexington, Massachusetts, on 24 November 2002.

moments.t: The Romans lay out Londinium as a civilian town about four years after the invasion of AD 43, at the lowest bridging point of the Thames.
Around AD 60 the Iceni under Boudica destroy the young settlement; it is rebuilt and becomes the provincial capital.
Between about 180 and 225 the Romans build the London Wall: roughly 3 km long, 6 m high and 2.5 m thick, the line the medieval city will keep.
William the Conqueror’s stone keep, the first stone castle in England, is begun about 1078 and largely finished by 1088.
The first stone bridge, begun in 1176, is completed in 1209 and carries houses and shops across the river for six hundred years.
The plague reaches London in the autumn of 1348 and peaks until May 1349; the city loses at least half of its population.
In Henry VIII’s reign London’s population reaches 100,000; by 1605 it is about 225,000 and the largest city in the kingdom by far.
The last great plague kills about 60,000 to 70,000 Londoners, roughly a fifth of the city.
From 2 to 5 September a fire that begins in Pudding Lane destroys about 60 per cent of the city, more than 13,000 buildings, Old St Paul’s and 87 parish churches, with few recorded deaths.
The new cathedral is topped out in 1708 and Parliament declares it complete on 25 December 1711; its dome stands over a city rebuilt in brick.
The first census counts 1,114,644 people in Greater London; the city grows from about a million in 1800 to 6.7 million a century later.
The London and Greenwich Railway, the first steam line in the capital, opens on 8 February 1836; Euston, the first mainline terminus, follows in 1837.
The Metropolitan Railway, the first underground line in the world, opens in 1863, in the same years that Bazalgette lays more than 2,100 km of sewers after the Great Stink of 1858.
German bombing from 7 September 1940 to 10 May 1941 opens a campaign that kills just under 30,000 Londoners by the end of the war.
Coal smoke trapped over the city in December 1952 kills an estimated 10,000 to 12,000 people and leads to the Clean Air Act.
Renzo Piano’s glass spire at London Bridge is inaugurated on 5 July 2012, three weeks before the Olympic Games open in Stratford.
When Henry Hudson sails the Half Moon into Upper New York Bay on 2 September 1609, some thousands of Lenape live in about 80 settlements around the harbour; Verrazzano had seen the bay in 1524.

moments.t: In 18 BC the kingdom of Baekje founds its capital Wiryeseong, believed to lie within modern Seoul; it stays the royal seat until 475.
King Sukjong of Goryeo builds a palace near the later Gyeongbokgung and names the town Namgyeong, the Southern Capital.
Yi Seong-gye chooses Hanyang in September 1394 and moves the capital from Kaesong; construction begins in October.
The main palace Gyeongbokgung and the royal ancestral shrine Jongmyo are built as the dynasty’s first works.
Taejo’s wall around the city, launched in 1395 and largely complete with its eight gates in 1396, is rebuilt in stone under Sejong and restored by Sukjong in 1704.
The second palace, Changdeokgung, is built east of the main palace.
In April 1592 the city is taken by the Japanese forces of Hideyoshi’s invasion.
In the years of the Korean Empire the first streetcar lines are laid and a railway links the capital to Incheon; the wall is breached for the tram lines.
After the annexation treaty of 1910 Japan renames the city Gyeongseong, Keijō in Japanese, and demotes it to the rank of other cities of Gyeonggi province.
The first post-liberation census counts 1,446,019 people.
The city falls to the North on 28 June 1950 as the Han River bridge is blown; it changes hands four times, and at least 191,000 buildings lie in ruins afterwards.
Two expansions in 1963 raise the city’s area from about 268 to 613 square kilometres and take in Gangnam south of the river.
The Seoul Metropolitan Subway begins operating in 1974; Line 1 replaces the Jongno streetcar.
Seoul hosts the Asian Games of 1986 and the Summer Olympics of 1988; the 63 Building of 1985 marks the new skyline of Yeouido.
The census of 1990 counts 10,612,577 people, the city’s peak.
The stream buried under an elevated road is uncovered and restored in 2005, three years after the city hosts the opening of the World Cup.
Ōta Dōkan builds a castle at Edo from 1457 on the site of the present Imperial Palace’s East Garden.
When Tokugawa Ieyasu first enters Edo in 1590 he finds a small fortified residence and no real town.
Ieyasu is appointed shogun in 1603 and sets up his headquarters at Edo Castle; Nihonbashi bridge is built the same year as the starting point of the highways.
The fire of 2 March 1657 burns a vast part of the city and kills about 100,000 people.

moments.t: The first census of 1721 counts about 1.3 million people; Edo had passed 500,000 in the 1650s and is by many estimates the largest city on earth.
The earthquake of 11 November 1855, magnitude 6.9 to 7.0, kills 8,000 to 10,000 people.
With the fall of the shogunate the city is renamed Tokyo in July 1868, and the emperor moves there in 1869; an estimated 360,000 daimyo retainers leave the city.

moments.t: A railway opens between Shinagawa and Yokohama in October 1872 and is extended to Shinbashi; after a fire the same year Ginza is rebuilt in brick to a design by Thomas Waters.
The earthquake of 1 September 1923 kills two to three per cent of a population of 4.5 million and leaves two million homeless.
The Tokyo Underground Railway begins operating between Asakusa and Ueno in 1927.
The raid of 9–10 March 1945 kills 90,000 to 100,000 people in a few hours and destroys a quarter of the city’s buildings.
The Tōkaidō Shinkansen begins operating and the Summer Olympics are held in October 1964; the population passes ten million the following year.
The broadcasting tower Skytree is completed in 2012.
Chosen in 2013 to host the 2020 Games, the city holds them in 2021 after the pandemic postponement.
Peter the Great founds the city on 27 May 1703; the Peter and Paul Fortress on Hare Island is its first building.
Peter moves the capital from Moscow to Saint Petersburg in 1712.
The Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences is established in 1724; the Kunstkamera is built by 1727.
Rastrelli’s Winter Palace is completed in 1762; the Hermitage collection is founded in 1764.
Falconet’s equestrian statue of Peter is unveiled in 1782.
The death of Alexander I is followed by the Decembrist revolt in Senate Square in December 1825.
The Moscow–Saint Petersburg railway begins operating in 1851.
Montferrand’s St Isaac’s Cathedral is completed in 1858.
The census of 1897 counts 1,267,023 people; by 1900 the city is the fourth largest in Europe.
The shooting of petitioners in January 1905 begins the revolution of 1905, which spreads from the city to the provinces.
The city is renamed Petrograd on the outbreak of the war in 1914.
The February Revolution ends the monarchy and the October Revolution overthrows the Provisional Government; some two million people leave the city in the following years.
On 24 January 1924, three days after Lenin’s death, Petrograd is renamed Leningrad.
From 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944 the city is besieged; more than a million civilians die.
The Leningrad Metro opens in 1955 with stations in marble and bronze.
A referendum on 12 June 1991 restores the original name, in force from 6 September.
Moscow is first recorded in 1147 as the place where Yuri Dolgoruky met Sviatoslav Olgovich.
The town is destroyed by the Mongols in the winter of 1237–38.
The seat of the Metropolitan of Rus is moved to Moscow, which rises over the other principalities.
The Kremlin citadel is founded in stone in 1367; it withstands sieges, including that of 1382.
The Dormition Cathedral is built in the Kremlin in 1479 by Aristotele Fioravanti.
Italian architects invited by Ivan III in the 1480s, among them Pietro Antonio Solari, build the Kremlin walls as they now stand, completed in 1495.
Moscow has about 100,000 people by 1500, 45,000 houses in 1520, and roughly doubles to 200,000 in the first half of the seventeenth century.
The Cathedral of the Intercession on the Moat, St Basil’s, is built on Red Square around 1560.
In 1571 the Crimean Tatars burn the city; the annals say only 30,000 of 200,000 inhabitants survive.
The militia of Minin and Pozharsky drives the Polish–Lithuanian garrison from the city.
Plague in 1771 is followed in September by a riot in which the crowd kills the archbishop.
When Napoleon enters in September 1812 the city burns; about three-quarters of it lies in ruins.
The 645 km railway to Saint Petersburg begins operating in 1851.
The city counts 1,023,817 people in 1900, having grown from 250,000 in 1812.
Lenin moves the capital back to Moscow on 12 March 1918.
The Moscow Metro opens on 15 May 1935; the city grows from one to ten million in the century.
By tradition recorded in Livy, Romulus founds the city in 753 BC.

moments.t: Greek colonists found Byzantium on the point between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara in 657 BC.

The land walls of Theodosius II are built in 413.
Begun after the Nika riots of 532, Justinian’s church is completed on 26 December 537; the city holds 300,000 to 500,000 people.
The plague of 541 kills about 40 per cent of the population.
The city withstands sieges in 674–678 and 717–718.
In April 1204 the crusaders take and thoroughly sack the city; it is recovered in 1261 with only about 35,000 people.
After a siege from 6 April, Mehmed II takes the city on 29 May 1453 and moves his capital here from Edirne.
The Grand Bazaar is built about 1460 and the Topkapı Palace begun in 1465; the Fatih Mosque follows in 1470.
Sinan’s mosque for Suleiman is completed in 1557.
The Blue Mosque is completed in 1616.
The first bridge across the Golden Horn is built in 1845.
Sirkeci railway station opens on 27 July 1872; the Orient Express from Paris begins running in 1883.
On 13 October 1923 the capital moves to Ankara; the city is renamed Istanbul in 1930.
The city counts 1,000,022 people in 1950, having reached 1,125,000 in 1914 before the losses of the war years.
The first bridge between Europe and Asia opens on 19 April 1973.
The Parisii, settled on the Seine since about 250 BC, are defeated by Labienus in 52 BC and the Roman town of Lutetia is laid out on the left bank.
Clovis makes Paris his capital in 508.
The Vikings besiege the city for a year in 885–886.
Construction of the new cathedral begins in 1163; the altar is consecrated in 1182.

moments.n: Philip Augustus’s wall and the Louvre
moments.t: Philip Augustus orders the first wall around the whole city in 1190 and builds the Louvre fortress between 1190 and 1202.
Innocent III charters the University of Paris in 1215; the Sorbonne opens in 1257.
Louis IX’s chapel for the Crown of Thorns is consecrated on 26 April 1248.
With about 200,000 people in 1328 Paris is the most populous city in Europe; the Black Death of 1348–49 kills 40,000 to 50,000.
On 24 August 1572 the bells of Saint-Germain l’Auxerrois signal the massacre of Protestants; about two thousand die by 30 August.
The Pont Neuf, begun in 1578, is finished between 1600 and 1607, the first bridge in the city without houses.
On 6 May 1682 the seat of the monarchy moves from the Tuileries to Versailles.
On 14 July 1789 the crowd storms the Bastille.
The cholera epidemic of 1832 kills about 18,500 to 20,000 people between March and October.
Napoleon III and his prefect Haussmann begin the reconstruction of the centre in 1853; the city has about a million people and annexes its suburbs in 1860.
After the Prussian siege of 1870–71 the Commune is crushed in the Bloody Week of 21–28 May 1871, with thousands of Communards killed.

moments.n: The Eiffel Tower and the Métro
moments.t: The 300-metre tower opens on 2 April 1889 for the Exposition; the first Métro line follows on 19 July 1900, and the population stands at 2,715,000 in 1901.
By a much later tradition the city is founded on 25 March 421; modern scholars do not accept the account.
After Pepin’s failed invasion of 810, Rialto comes to prominence over the other lagoon settlements and becomes Venice proper.
Mark the Evangelist is designated patron of the city in 828.
The basilica is consecrated in 1094.
After the sack of Constantinople monuments and works of art are carried to Venice.

moments.n: The closing of the Great Council
moments.t: The Serrata of 1297 fixes the ruling families.

A printing press is in operation in 1469; Aldus follows in the 1490s.
The census of 1548 counts 158,069 people, the city near its peak.
Plague strikes again in 1575–77.
The wooden bridge of 1173 is replaced in stone in 1591.
The Italian plague of 1629–31 strikes Venice.
The Republic falls in 1797 and a Provisional Municipality is set up under the French.
The Milan–Venice railway begins operating in 1842, bringing the mainland to the lagoon.
The first Venice Biennale opens on 30 April 1895.
On 4 November 1966 the highest acqua alta on record floods the city.
A Roman colony is founded about 59 BC.
The commune is adopted and the Republic of Florence established in 1115–16.
The mint is established and the gold florin introduced in 1252.
The third ring of walls is built in 1284.
