The Ponte Vecchio is rebuilt in 1345.
The plague strikes the city in 1348.
The revolt of the wool-workers runs from 1378 to 1382.
Cosimo comes to power on 6 October 1434.
The dome of Santa Maria del Fiore is completed and the cathedral consecrated in 1436.
Piero II flees before Charles VIII and the Republic is restored; Savonarola is executed on 23 May 1498.
The siege of Florence begins on 24 October 1529.
Vasari begins the Uffizi in 1560; it is finished in 1581.
The capital of Italy moves from Turin to Florence in 1865; the census of 1861 counts 150,864 people.
On 4 November 1966 the Arno floods the city.
Vindobona is settled about AD 100; the first mention of Vienna by name comes in 881.
Henry II of Austria makes Vienna his capital in 1155.
St Stephen’s is built from about 1160; the tower is rebuilt in the 1860s.
The University of Vienna is founded in 1365.
The Turks besiege Vienna in 1529.
The great plague of Vienna strikes in 1679.
The second Ottoman siege ends with the battle of 1683.
The city has 150,000 people in 1724 and 200,000 by 1790.
The revolution of 1848 reaches Vienna.
The walls come down and the Ring Road is built from 1858; the Opera opens in 1869 and the World Exposition is held in 1873.
The census of 1880 counts 1,090,119 people.
The giant wheel of the Prater is erected in 1897.
The population reaches 2,031,000 in 1910, its peak.
Red Vienna begins in 1918.
Germany annexes Austria in 1938; the Vienna Offensive of 1945 ends the war in the city.
The Vienna International Centre opens in 1979, three years after the U-Bahn.
The earliest settlement near the Gihon Spring dates to 4500–3500 BC; the name appears in Egyptian execration texts about 2000 BC.
David captures the city about 1010 BC and makes it his capital.
Solomon builds the First Temple about 962 BC.
In 587–586 BC the Babylonians destroy the city and the First Temple.
The Second Temple is completed in 516 BC, in the sixth year of Darius.
Herod expands the Temple Mount and rebuilds the Temple from 19 BC.
Titus ends the main phase of the Jewish war and destroys Herod’s Temple in AD 70; Hadrian refounds the city as Aelia Capitolina in 136.
After Helena’s visit in 326 the first Church of the Holy Sepulchre is built in 335.
Caliph Umar takes the city in 636–637, after the Persian sack of 614.
Abd al-Malik builds the Dome of the Rock between 687 and 691.
The First Crusade takes the city in 1099 and slaughters much of its Muslim and Jewish population.
Saladin takes the city from the Crusaders in 1187.
Suleiman the Magnificent rebuilds the walls between 1535 and 1538.
General Allenby enters Jerusalem on foot in December 1917, weeks after the Balfour Declaration; the British Mandate follows in 1920.
The war of 1948 divides the city; West Jerusalem is proclaimed Israeli territory in July and the east is annexed by Jordan in 1950.
Israeli forces take the Old City on 7 June 1967 and declare the city unified on 28 June.
Solon’s laws are established in 594 BC.
The Persians burn the city in 480 and 479 BC.
Construction of the Parthenon begins in 447 BC.

moments.n: The Peloponnesian War and the plague
moments.t: The war with Sparta begins in 431 BC; the plague strikes in 430.
Athens is defeated in the Peloponnesian War in 404 BC.
Roman forces sack the city in the 80s BC.
The Agora is sacked by the Heruli in 267.
The Ottomans take the city in 1456.
The Venetians under Morosini besiege the city in 1687.
The marbles are taken to Britain from 1801.
Athens becomes the capital of the kingdom in 1834; the university is founded in 1837.
The Games of 1896 are held in the city.
More than a million Greek refugees from Asia Minor settle in and around Athens; the metropolis counts 802,000 by 1928.
The metropolitan population reaches 1,124,109 in 1940.
Clashes in December 1944 open the road to civil war.
The Summer Olympics and Paralympics are held in 2004, with the metro extended in 2000.
Alexander renames the village of Rhacotis Alexandria about 331 BC.
Ptolemy proclaims himself king in 305 BC.
The Library opens about 283 BC.
The lighthouse is built about 247 BC.
Caesar takes the city in 48 BC and the great library burns.
After the battle of 30 BC Antony and Cleopatra die and Augustus takes the city.
Theodosius orders the destruction of the pagan temples in 391; Hypatia is lynched in 415.
The Arabs take the city in 641–642 and move the capital to Fustat.
Earthquakes in 1303 and 1323 bring down the lighthouse.
The French take the city in 1798; the British in 1801. By 1800 only about 8,000 people live there.
The canal to the Nile is built in 1819 and the port revives.
The Cairo–Alexandria railway begins operating in 1856.
The city counts 60,000 in 1840 and 170,000 by 1863.
The city counts 919,024 in 1947 and about 1.5 million by 1965.
The new library is inaugurated in 2002.
Al-Mansur begins the Round City in 762.
Harun al-Rashid comes to power in 786.
The civil war between al-Amin and al-Ma’mun ends in a siege of the city.
The caliphate moves to Samarra in 836 and returns in 892.
The Seljuks take power in 1055; the Nizamiyya college is founded in 1067.
The Mustansiriya madrasa is founded in 1232.
In January–February 1258 Hulagu’s forces destroy the city and kill most of its population.
Timur captures the city again in 1401.
The city becomes the capital of the Ottoman eyalet of Baghdad in 1535; the Safavids hold it from 1623 until Murad IV retakes it in 1638.
Flood and famine strike in 1831.
The city is estimated at 100,000 people in 1895.
The British take the city in March 1917; it becomes the capital of the Mandate in 1920.
The coup of 14 July 1958 ends the monarchy; the city is capital of the Republic.
The city counts 1,490,759 people in 1965.
The bombing of 1991 includes the Amiriyah shelter on 13 February.
The battle of Baghdad is fought on 3–12 April 2003.
The mosque of Amr ibn al-As is built in 642 at Fustat, the first Muslim capital of Egypt.
Ahmad ibn Tulun founds al-Qata’i in 873 and his mosque is built in 879.
The Fatimid caliph al-Mu’izz founds Misr al-Qahira in 970; al-Azhar is established the same year.
The city wall and the gates, among them Bab Zuwayla and Bab al-Nasr, are built in 1092.
The Citadel is built in 1183.
The city becomes the capital of the Mamluk Sultanate in 1250.
Ottoman forces take Cairo in 1517 and it becomes a provincial capital.
Napoleon arrives in 1798; the city has about 200,000 people in 1800.
The mosque on the Citadel is built in 1848.
The railway station is built in 1856.
The opera house opens in 1869 for the Suez Canal celebrations, in Ismail’s new quarters.
The census of 1947 counts 2,090,654 people (654,476 in 1907).
The fire of January 1952 burns the European quarter; Ismailia Square is renamed Tahrir.
The tower is built in 1961.
Line 1 of the Cairo Metro begins operating in 1987.
The uprising against the Mubarak regime begins on 25 January 2011.
The city government dates the grants of Ji and Yan by King Wu of Zhou to 1045 BC.
The Liao rename Youzhou Nanjing, the Southern Capital, in 938; 22,000 people live inside the walls.
The Jin move their capital here in 1153 and name it Zhongdu, the Central Capital.
After a long siege the city surrenders in 1215 and is looted and burned.
Kublai Khan begins Dadu in 1267 and names it capital of the Yuan in 1271; the city counts 952,000 by 1327.
Xu Da captures Dadu in 1368 and it is renamed Beiping.
The Yongle Emperor builds the Forbidden City from 1406 to 1420 and moves the capital from Nanjing in 1421.
The Outer City wall is built in 1553.
On 3 May 1644 the Manchus seize Beijing.
Anglo-French forces take the city and Lord Elgin orders the Old Summer Palace burned.
Boxers and Qing troops besiege the Legation Quarter in June 1900; foreign armies lift the siege and occupy the city.
Students gather in Tiananmen Square on 4 May 1919; in 1928 the capital moves to Nanjing and the city is renamed Beiping.
Mao proclaims the People’s Republic from Tiananmen Gate on 1 October 1949; the city has just over two million people.
The Ming walls are demolished in the 1960s for the subway, which begins trial operation in 1969, and the 2nd Ring Road.
The protests of spring 1989 end in the military crackdown of 3–4 June.
The Games open on 8 August 2008 at the National Stadium; the city counts 13.56 million in 2000 and 20.18 million by 2011.
Emperor Kanmu arrives on 22 October 794 and names the city Heian-kyō on 8 November; it is laid out on the grid of Chang’an, 4.5 by 5.2 km, without walls.
The East and West temples on the southern edge are the only temples permitted within the city.
The Golden Pavilion is founded in 1397.
The war of 1467–77 burns almost half the city, which does not fully recover until the mid-sixteenth century.
In the late sixteenth century Hideyoshi lays out new streets and raises the earthwork walls called odoi.
The great Kyoto fire of 1788 destroys most of the city.
The fighting of 1864 burns down 28,000 houses.
The imperial court moves to Tokyo in 1869; the modern city is formed on 1 April 1889 with 279,165 people.
The railway station opens in 1877.
The canal, begun in 1885, is completed on 9 April 1890.
Kyoto introduces the country’s first commercial electric railway, powered by the canal, and builds the Heian Shrine for the city’s eleven-hundredth anniversary.
The population exceeds one million in 1932.
Removed from the atomic target list and largely spared from bombing, the city keeps its temples.
The tower is erected in 1964.
The city hosts the conference that produces the protocol on greenhouse gases, and the new Kyoto Station opens.
Anangpal Tomar founds Lal Kot in 1052; the Chauhans take it in 1180 and rename it Qila Rai Pithora.
Muhammad Ghori defeats Prithviraj at Tarain in 1192 and sacks the city; the Qutb Minar is begun.
From 1206 Delhi is the capital of the Sultanate under Qutb-ud-din Aibak.
Timur enters the city on 18 December 1398; it is sacked and left in ruins.
Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 and founds the Mughal dynasty.
Shah Jahan moves the capital back to Delhi and builds the walled city with the Red Fort; it becomes the capital in 1648.
Nadir Shah sacks the city and a two-day massacre kills over 30,000.
The Company defeats the Marathas at the battle of Delhi in 1803.
British forces besiege the city from 8 June 1857 and take it on 21 September; the last Mughal is exiled.
At the Durbar of 1911 George V announces the move of the capital from Calcutta.
Lutyens’ New Delhi is inaugurated in 1931.
About 500,000 Hindu and Sikh refugees come to Delhi and about 300,000 Muslims leave for Pakistan.
The Delhi Metro begins operation in 2002.
Delhi hosts the Games in 2010; the census of 2011 counts 16,753,235 people.
The Mexica found the island city about 1325 where, in the legend, an eagle with a snake perches on a cactus.
The empire is formed in 1428; the Templo Mayor to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc rises at its centre.

moments.n: The largest city in the Americas
moments.t: Causeways and two aqueducts from Chapultepec serve a city of more than 200,000 fed by chinampas.
Cortés enters Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519.
After a siege from 22 May the city falls on 13 August 1521 and is rebuilt as the Spanish capital.
The Royal and Pontifical University is founded in the early 1550s.
Construction of the cathedral starts in 1573 and is completed in 1813.
Rains inundate the capital in 1629 and the waters remain for years.
In 1692 a crowd burns the viceroy’s palace.
The city counts 112,926 people in 1790.
The Army of the Three Guarantees enters the city on 21 September 1821.
US forces take the city in September 1847; French troops occupy it in 1863.
The palace, begun under Díaz, is inaugurated in 1934.
The massacre of 2 October 1968 precedes the Games by ten days; the Metro opens in 1969.
The earthquake of 19 September 1985 devastates the centre.
The city proper counts 9,209,944 people in 2020, from 2,233,709 in 1950.
The Killke people occupy the valley from 900 to 1200 and build the first fortress at Sacsayhuamán about 1100.
By legend Manco Cápac founds the city in the twelfth century; the Inca expand Sacsayhuamán in the thirteenth.
Pachacuti, who comes to power in 1438, is credited with the city’s design in the shape of a puma, Sacsayhuamán at its head.
Pizarro takes possession of the city on 15 November 1533.
The city is re-established on 23 March 1534 with its first alcaldes.
Manco Inca besieges the city from May 1536; the fight for Sacsayhuamán is fought on 14 May.
The Iglesia del Triunfo is built in 1539; the basilica is built from 1560 and consecrated in the eighteenth century.
The earthquake of 31 March 1650 destroys almost all the colonial buildings.
The rebellion besieges the city in 1781; its leader is executed in the Plaza de Armas.
Independence is proclaimed in Cusco on 3 August 1814; Pumacahua is executed in 1815.
The city has 47,000 people in the 1840s.
The earthquake of 21 May 1950 damages more than a third of the city.
UNESCO lists the City of Cusco in 1983.
The census of 2017 counts 428,450 people.
Pizarro founds the Ciudad de los Reyes on 18 January 1535 and construction of the cathedral begins.
Pizarro is assassinated on 26 June 1541.
The university of San Marcos, the first in the city, is founded in 1551; the first printing press arrives in 1584.
The cathedral is consecrated in 1625.
The walls built in 1684–87 enclose a city that the earthquakes of October and December 1687 largely destroy.
The earthquake of 28 October 1746 severely damages the city and destroys Callao.
San Martín’s forces enter and independence is declared in 1821.
The Lima–Callao line is completed about 1850.
The city walls are torn down in the early 1870s.
The census of 1876 counts 101,488 people.
Chilean troops occupy the city from 1881 to 1883.
An earthquake hits the city on 24 May 1940; the population is about 600,000.
The urban agglomeration counts 1,436,231 in 1961.
The historic centre is listed by UNESCO in 1988.
The city counts 10,039,455 people in 2016.
Rui de Sequeira names the lagoon for Portugal about 1472; the Awori settle the island of Eko.
About 1600 the Oba of Benin appoints the Awori chief Ashipa ruler of Eko; tribute to Benin lasts until 1830.
Akinsemoyin opens the kingdom to the slave trade in the 1760s; by the early nineteenth century Eko is the largest slave exporter in the northern hemisphere.
Britain bombards Lagos in 1851, installs Akitoye and in 1852 signs a treaty abolishing the slave trade.
Oba Dosunmu signs the Treaty of Cession on 6 August 1861; Lagos is declared a colony on 5 March 1862.
Electric street lighting begins on 19 September 1898.
The railway to Ibadan opens on 4 March 1901 and the Carter Bridge joins the island to the mainland.
Lagos becomes the capital of the amalgamated Colony and Protectorate on 1 January 1914.
The census of 1931 counts 126,474 people (98,303 in 1921).
Lagos remains the capital when Nigeria becomes independent in 1960.
Lagos State is created in 1967; the state capital moves to Ikeja in 1976.
The city counts 1,060,848 people in 1975.
The bridge opens in 1990.
The federal government moves to Abuja in 1991.
The urban agglomeration is estimated at 8,767,000 in 2005; Eko Atlantic begins in 2013.
